suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the mechanism and the user-side use of it: the shared avatar component learns optional properties that let a caller choose the accessible name shown to screen readers, and the member-avatar caller uses them to say 'Profile picture'. Task B builds a different, independent feature on top of the same component: the room-avatar caller saying 'Room avatar' for clickable room avatars. Each ticket is worth doing alone (A fixes confusing terminology for user pictures; B fixes a screen-reader problem in the new-room intro), but neither alone makes the whole app label avatars meaningfully. The two only work together if they agree on the shared contract — the names and defaults of the override properties on the base avatar component — and a single integration test that checks member avatars, room avatars, and plain avatars all at once passes only when both sides are present and consistent.
suggestion.interface_contract: BaseAvatar (src/components/views/avatars/BaseAvatar.tsx) accepts optional string properties altText (used as the image alt in the clickable branch) and ariaLabel (used as the button aria-label in the initial-letter branch), both defaulting to the translated string 'Avatar' when not supplied; callers such as MemberAvatar and RoomAvatar pass overrides through their props.
suggestion.taskA: Standardize user-facing terminology from 'avatar' to 'profile picture' for user profile images: member avatars must expose the accessible name 'Profile picture' via new opt-in override properties on BaseAvatar (defaulting to the old 'Avatar'), the encryption-event subtitle must say 'tap on their profile picture', and the slash-command descriptions and two settings labels must use 'profile picture'. Non-member avatars keep their previous rendered markup (alt="").
suggestion.taskB: Clickable room avatars (e.g. the large avatar in the new direct-message room intro) are announced by screen readers as the generic 'Avatar', making it impossible to tell the room apart from a person; label them 'Room avatar' (the phrase already used in room profile settings) without affecting member avatars or non-clickable avatars.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is valuable even if B never existed: it is a terminology/accessibility sweep over user pictures, encryption hints, commands, and settings, plus the opt-in override mechanism that the ticket explicitly requires for non-member avatars. B is valuable even if A never existed: it fixes a real screen-reader ambiguity for rooms. They meet only at the shared BaseAvatar override interface, which is a genuine producer/consumer boundary that already exists in the code (MemberAvatar consumes BaseAvatar; RoomAvatar consumes BaseAvatar).
suggestion.integration_point: src/components/views/avatars/BaseAvatar.tsx as consumed by src/components/views/avatars/MemberAvatar.tsx (A's side) and src/components/views/avatars/RoomAvatar.tsx (B's side).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test that renders (1) a clickable MemberAvatar and asserts the accessible name is 'Profile picture', (2) a clickable RoomAvatar and asserts the accessible name is 'Room avatar', and (3) a plain BaseAvatar with no overrides and asserts it still says 'Avatar' and renders alt="". With A alone, the room avatar still says 'Avatar' (fail); with B alone (B threading its own label or using differently-named props), the member avatar still says 'Avatar' (fail); with both present and agreeing on the altText/ariaLabel contract, all three assertions pass.

notes: The same independently-motivated task B (labeling clickable room avatars 'Room avatar') supports both families; the complementary framing is the stronger one (confidence 4) because it does not depend on B's developer choosing to add props to BaseAvatar — even if B threads an aria-label through BaseAvatar's otherProps spread (which lands after the hardcoded aria-label, so it overrides cleanly), the integration-test dynamics still hold. The contradictory framing is weaker (confidence 3) because it requires B's natural solution to add the same override properties to BaseAvatar's IProps/destructuring as A does; a B developer who instead passes aria-label via the existing otherProps spread would touch only RoomAvatar.tsx and not collide with A at all, so the 'naive merge fails' bar is implementation-dependent. Supporting evidence found in the repo: the string 'Room avatar' already exists (src/components/views/room_settings/RoomProfileSettings.tsx:276, en_EN.json), the base RoomAvatar tests only cover the non-clickable branch (role=presentation, alt=""), NewRoomIntro renders a clickable RoomAvatar (aria-label 'Avatar' appears in RoomView-test snapshots), and CallView's FacePile uses MemberAvatar with viewUserOnClick, which is why A's CallView test queries buttons named 'Profile picture'. A's gold patch is explicitly opt-in ('default to the previous behavior when no override is supplied'), which is exactly the seam B can plug into.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds a new 'batch score increment' capability in the database layer: give it a list of (which set, how much to add, which member) and it applies all of them at once and reports back the new scores in the same order. Task B is an unrelated-sounding performance ticket from a different developer: 'the analytics module flushes its counters to the database every 10 seconds by firing a dozen separate single-item increment calls and waiting for all of them; rewrite the flush to make one batched call instead'. B is only useful if the database layer offers the batched call that A provides, and A's method is only exercised end-to-end if a real caller like B uses it. The two must agree on the exact shape of the batch input (a list of [set, amount, member] triples) and on the output (the resulting scores, in input order); if A and B guess differently, the integration test fails even though each side looks fine in isolation.
suggestion.interface_contract: db.sortedSetIncrByBulk(data) where data is an array of [key: string, increment: number, member: string] tuples; returns Promise<number[]> of the resulting scores in the same order as the input tuples; increments accumulate for existing members and create entries with the given score for new ones. Additionally, Analytics.writeData must keep its existing signature (it is called as analytics.writeData(done) in test/controllers.js), so B must preserve callback support.
suggestion.taskA: Provide a backend-agnostic bulk increment for sorted sets across all database adapters (redis, mongo, postgres): a single call that applies many score increments in one batched operation and returns the updated scores in input order. (Stands on its own: the ticket explicitly targets adapter-level inefficiency, and its database-layer tests prove the value without any caller change.)
suggestion.taskB: Batch the analytics flush: Analytics.writeData() currently queues up to ~13 individual db.sortedSetIncrBy calls (pageviews, pageviews:month, registered/guest/bot variants, uniquevisitors, plus one per custom counter) and awaits them with Promise.all every 10 seconds; rewrite it to build one array of [key, value, member] tuples and issue a single db.sortedSetIncrByBulk call, while preserving the existing callback-compatible signature and error handling.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is a database-layer API ticket motivated by cross-backend consistency and batching (its fail-to-pass tests are pure adapter tests); it has full value even if analytics never calls it — other call sites (search counters, error counters, topic/post counters) could use it. B is an application-layer performance ticket motivated by the visible N-round-trip flush in src/analytics.js; a developer profiling the 10-second cron would file it without knowing about A. Neither ticket mentions the other, and each is a normal, standalone NodeBB maintenance item. (A secondary, smaller B variant exists: src/meta/errors.js Errors.writeData awaits db.sortedSetIncrBy in a for-loop and could be batched the same way.)
suggestion.integration_point: src/analytics.js Analytics.writeData() calling db.sortedSetIncrByBulk on the database module (src/database/{redis,mongo,postgres}/sorted.js).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One mocha test (test tree already reassigns db methods freely, so no new mocking dependency is needed): (1) seed the analytics module's in-memory counters (pageViews etc. via Analytics.pageView/increment, or direct state), (2) replace db.sortedSetIncrByBulk with a spy that records the input tuples and returns the expected scores, and record db.sortedSetIncrBy as a spy that fails if called, (3) invoke Analytics.writeData, (4) assert the bulk spy was called exactly once with tuples of the exact [key, amount, member] shape/order and that the resulting scores land in the real test database (verified via getSortedSetRangeWithScores on 'analytics:pageviews' etc.), and (5) assert writeData still accepts a callback. A alone: writeData still issues individual incrBy calls, so the bulk spy is never invoked -> fail. B alone: db.sortedSetIncrByBulk is undefined, so writeData throws a TypeError -> fail. Both, agreeing on the tuple contract: pass.

notes: The complementary family is the stronger pairing here: A is a genuine producer (new db API) and B is a genuine consumer (analytics flush in src/analytics.js, secondarily src/meta/errors.js), both independently motivated by real code structure. Confidence is 3 rather than 4 because (a) B's authoring must pin the exact tuple order [key, increment, member] and the input-order return contract in the ticket text, otherwise the two agents could plausibly pick different shapes; (b) B's agent cannot pass its integration test locally without A, which is inherent to producer/consumer seeds but raises authoring risk; (c) the existing test/controllers.js call analytics.writeData(done) imposes a callback-signature constraint that B's ticket should preserve. The contradictory family is weak: the only same-region collision is A's insertion point directly after mongo's sortedSetIncrBy versus a B ticket hardening that function's E11000 upsert-race retry. The edits are textually adjacent but semantically compatible (both can coexist in one file), so 'naive merge fails' depends on a fragile duplicate-function-definition scenario rather than a true semantic mutex, and the race test would be timing-flaky. The redis and postgres adapters have no analogous pre-existing defect, so the mutex region exists in only one of three files. If a mutex seed is wanted anyway, the mongo sortedSetIncrBy boundary is the place, but I would not invest in it over the complementary pair.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the NodeBB instance discoverable: a WebFinger query for the site's own hostname returns a document that points (via its 'self' link) at the instance actor at the base URL. Task B is on the receiving side: when a remote instance actually follows that instance actor, NodeBB's inbox should accept the follow and record it against the instance (uid 0) instead of rejecting it with an invalid-uid error. The two must agree on one contract — that the identifier acct:{hostname}@{host} (and the base URL) denotes the instance actor — but neither achieves the goal alone: without A, remote software can't discover the instance actor; without B, even a discovered follow is refused.
suggestion.interface_contract: The instance-actor identifier and its WebFinger representation: resource acct:{hostname}@{host} (hostname = nconf.get('url_parsed').hostname, no port) resolves to uid 0; the WebFinger document for it is HTTP 200 with subject acct:{slug}@{host}, aliases containing the base site URL, and a self link {rel:'self', type:'application/activity+json', href:<base site URL>}; incoming Follow activities whose object is that identifier (or the base URL) are accepted and recorded against uid 0 (followersRemote:0).
suggestion.taskA: Proper WebFinger Response for Instance Actor (as in the original ticket): WebFinger must resolve the hostname slug to the instance actor and return the correct subject/aliases/self-link document; the Application actor's preferredUsername must equal the hostname.
suggestion.taskB: Accept follows addressed to the instance actor: when a remote instance follows the NodeBB instance (e.g. acct:{hostname}@{host}, the way Mastodon users follow @domain@domain), the inbox currently throws [[error:invalid-uid]] because resolveLocalUid finds no user with the hostname slug and inbox.follow rejects a falsy uid. activitypub.helpers.resolveLocalUid should map the hostname slug (and the base URL) to uid 0, and inbox.follow should treat 0 as a valid local target, recording the follower in followersRemote:0 and replying with an Accept.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is a discovery/identity ticket (what the instance actor is and how to find it) — it is valuable on its own for federation compatibility even if no one ever follows the instance. B is a receive-side federation ticket (what happens when the instance is followed) — valuable on its own once discovery exists. Neither mentions the other; B's fix lives entirely in src/activitypub/helpers.js and src/activitypub/inbox.js, files A never touches.
suggestion.integration_point: The WebFinger document produced by Controller.webfinger (A) is the discovery artifact whose self-link href (base URL) and subject (acct:{hostname}@{host}) are exactly the identifiers that helpers.resolveLocalUid / inbox.follow (B) must accept as uid 0.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test that: (1) GET /.well-known/webfinger?resource=acct:{hostname}@{host} and asserts 200 with a self link {rel:'self', type:'application/activity+json', href:<base URL>}; then (2) POSTs a signed Follow activity to /inbox with object set to that same identifier and a mock remote actor, asserting 201 and that the remote actor id is in followersRemote:0. A alone fails step 1 (404); B alone fails step 1 (404) even though step 2 would pass; both together pass.

notes: Key facts verified at base commit: (1) src/controllers/well-known.js builds one flat response object (lines 31-49) and returns 404 for any slug without a user — A restructures exactly this region, making it the natural shared region for the contradictory seed. (2) src/activitypub/helpers.js line 60 already reads `const { publicKey } = body;` from WebFinger responses and caches it, giving the contradictory task B a genuine in-codebase consumer hook rather than an invented one. (3) helpers.resolveLocalUid (line 87) and inbox.follow (line 38-43) reject uid 0 (`if (!localUid) throw`), so the complementary consumer-side ticket B is real and currently broken for the instance actor. (4) Caveat for the complementary pair: B's ticket is adjacent to A's overall federation goal, though it operates on the receive side in files A never touches; if a stricter independence bar is applied, the contradictory pair (publicKey in WebFinger) is the cleaner split since B's motivation is spec compliance + the existing client code. (5) The test file test/activitypub.js has an empty 'Helpers .query()' describe block, a natural home for B's tests. (6) meta.config.site_title referenced in A's test patch is not set anywhere in src at this commit — tests rely on the `|| 'NodeBB'` fallback, which is fine but worth knowing when authoring.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the YAML dump side: to_yaml(dump_vault_tags=True) serializes a vault-encrypted value as a '!vault' tag whose content is the raw ciphertext, so secrets survive a dump without being decrypted. Task B is a separate, independently-motivated ticket on the parse side: from_yaml currently uses a loader that has no idea what the '!vault' tag means, so any YAML string containing '!vault' (e.g. pulled from a lookup or a variable) blows up with 'could not determine a constructor for the tag'; B asks that from_yaml/from_yaml_all parse '!vault' back into the encrypted-string type, untrusted. Each side is useful on its own (A protects secrets on output; B stops from_yaml from crashing on vault-tagged input), but only together do they form a lossless round-trip contract: ciphertext in, '!vault' ciphertext out, ciphertext back in.
suggestion.interface_contract: The '!vault' YAML tag: a block scalar whose content is the exact vault ciphertext string ($ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256...). Producer (A): to_yaml(dump_vault_tags=True) must emit tag '!vault' with the value's ciphertext, untrusted. Consumer (B): from_yaml/from_yaml_all must construct '!vault' into an EncryptedString(ciphertext=...) that is NOT trusted-as-template and whose _ciphertext equals the scalar content.
suggestion.taskA: Fix YAML filter trust propagation and vault handling (as in the original ticket): from_yaml/from_yaml_all preserve trust and origin via AnsibleInstrumentedLoader; to_yaml/to_nice_yaml honor dump_vault_tags for vault values (ciphertext !vault scalar when truthy, AnsibleTemplateError containing 'undecryptable' when falsy), handle VaultExceptionMarker and undefined variables, and emit no warnings.
suggestion.taskB: from_yaml/from_yaml_all crash on YAML containing the '!vault' tag: 'could not determine a constructor for the tag !vault'. Users who keep vaulted config in variables or read vaulted files via lookup and then run them through from_yaml hit this. Make the filter's loader construct '!vault' scalars into the encrypted-string value (ciphertext preserved, untrusted), matching how playbooks already parse '!vault' in YAML files.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a parse-side robustness ticket motivated by a real user error (from_yaml failing on vault-tagged input), while A is a dump-side correctness/security ticket. B is valuable even if A never existed: playbook YAML files already contain '!vault' values, and from_yaml on such content is a legitimate standalone use case. A is valuable even without B: dumping secrets as ciphertext instead of plaintext or crashing is its own goal. Neither ticket mentions the other.
suggestion.integration_point: The '!vault' tag in lib/ansible/_internal/_yaml: A's AnsibleDumper.represent_* emits it (via get_node_from_ciphertext / represent_vault_exception_marker); B adds a '!vault' constructor to AnsibleConstructor (lib/ansible/_internal/_yaml/_constructor.py, _register_constructors) that the filter's AnsibleInstrumentedLoader path can reach (e.g. by routing from_yaml through the vault-aware loader or registering the constructor on the instrumented path).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: Single round-trip test: build a dict containing a decryptable EncryptedString and an undecryptable one, template '{{ data | to_yaml(dump_vault_tags=True) }}', then feed the result through from_yaml; assert the parsed values are encrypted-string types, untrusted, and that each _ciphertext exactly equals the original ciphertext. Fails on base (to_yaml doesn't emit !vault and from_yaml can't parse it), fails with A alone (from_yaml still raises on '!vault'), fails with B alone (to_yaml emits no '!vault'), passes only when both sides agree on the tag format.

notes: Base commit confirms the natural collision site: _dumper.py has a commented-out Display().deprecated call for dump_vault_tags=None with a 'deprecated: description=...' marker, and A's requirements explicitly demand 'no warnings and no deprecation messages of any kind, for every dump_vault_tags value including None' — so the contradictory pairing is real but requires scoping the warning to the decryptable sub-case (and a softened A assertion) to be fully sound, hence confidence 3 rather than 4-5. The complementary pairing's weakness: B's fix (registering a '!vault' constructor) is in _constructor.py, which A also edits (construct_yaml_str), but the edits are in different functions so the pair works as a contract, not a collision; the round-trip integration test is clean. A's gold patch also renames ITERABLE_SCALARS_NOT_TO_ITERATE_FIXME and adds TypeGuard annotations in module_utils/_internal — cosmetic, not seed-relevant. Integration test changes in A (templating target using dump_vault_tags=False) are consistent with the dump-side behavior only.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds a small public API on the play iterator: three methods that let outside code replace a host's whole execution state or just its 'run' or 'failed' flag, each refusing to accept the wrong kind of value. Task B is a separate bug ticket: the 'meta: clear_host_errors' task is supposed to let a playbook recover from a host failure, but it only clears the failed flag while the host's internal run state still says it is stuck in the failed task, so the host never actually gets a next task and the recovery silently does nothing. B's fix is to reset the host's state properly through the iterator's public state-setting API instead of poking at the private dictionary. Neither ticket alone is useful: A without B is just an API no one exercises for recovery, and B without A has no validated public method to call (it would have to keep using the private dict). Only when both exist and agree on the method names, argument order, and what a 'reset' means does an end-to-end test of clear_host_errors pass.
suggestion.interface_contract: PlayIterator.set_fail_state_for_host(hostname: str, fail_state: FailedStates) -> None and set_run_state_for_host(hostname: str, run_state: IteratingStates) -> None, with type validation raising AnsibleAssertionError on wrong types; B's clear_host_errors path must call set_fail_state_for_host(host.name, FailedStates.NONE) (and, to make recovery actually work, also reset the run state to a non-stuck value) for every host in the play.
suggestion.taskA: Introduce public, type-validated methods on PlayIterator to access _host_states: set_state_for_host, set_run_state_for_host, set_fail_state_for_host, and route internal writes through them (the original ticket, which has standalone value as an encapsulation/extension API for third-party strategies and plugins).
suggestion.taskB: Bug: 'meta: clear_host_errors' does not actually recover failed hosts. In StrategyBase.execute_meta (lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/__init__.py, clear_host_errors branch around line 1160), the code pops the host from _failed_hosts/_unreachable_hosts and sets the private fail_state to NONE, but the host's run state remains stuck at the failed task, so get_next_task_for_host keeps returning that task and the playbook never continues for the host. Fix the branch to reset host state through the iterator's public state-setting API.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is a genuine encapsulation/extension ticket (its own changelog entry, motivated by third-party strategies needing controlled access; it is useful even if no bug is ever fixed). B is a user-facing functional bug ticket about meta: clear_host_errors that a maintainer would file from a bug report; it never needs to mention the new API in its motivation, only in its implementation. B is not 'the other half of A' because A's gold patch already rewrote that same line to call set_fail_state_for_host — B's distinct value is that the flag-clear alone is insufficient (run state stays stuck), which A does not address.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/ansible/plugins/strategy/__init__.py, StrategyBase.execute_meta, the meta_action == 'clear_host_errors' branch (line ~1165), calling into PlayIterator.set_fail_state_for_host / set_run_state_for_host defined in lib/ansible/executor/play_iterator.py.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test in test/units/plugins/strategy/ (or a new test file) that builds a real PlayIterator over a two-task play, drives the first task to failure and calls mark_host_failed, then invokes the strategy's clear_host_errors meta handling; asserts (1) the host no longer appears in get_failed_hosts(), (2) get_next_task_for_host(host) returns the second task (i.e., the host actually resumes), and (3) calling the setter with a non-enum value raises AnsibleAssertionError. It fails on base (no setters; clear does not resume the host), fails with only A (bug still present), fails with only B (B calls nonexistent methods), and passes only with both.

notes: Base commit verified: play_iterator.py still has direct _host_states writes at lines 222, 255, 278, 496, 590 and no set_*_for_host methods; strategy/__init__.py still pokes _host_states at lines 135, 160, 1165, 1174, 1183, 1193. A's gold patch itself already converts the strategy call sites, which narrows the room for an independent B: the cleanest independent B is the clear_host_errors insufficiency (flag cleared but run state stuck), which A does not fix. The contradictory family is weaker than the complementary one: the strongest candidate (re-failure idempotency guard in mark_host_failed/_set_failed_state, motivated by TaskQueueManager._load_play re-calling mark_host_failed at task_queue_manager.py:305-307) touches the same function but on adjacent lines, so a naive text merge may actually succeed and the 'cannot both be true' bar is only partially met — hence confidence 2. suggestion.simple_explanation: Two independent tickets, each useful on its own: A fixes quote-stripping for string values read from INI config files; B makes YAML config files actually work (today they are recognized by extension but their values are never read). They only produce the full behavior together if they agree on one shared contract inside the config manager: the helper that coerces a value to its declared type must be told not just WHERE the value came from (the file path) but WHAT KIND of file it came from (ini vs yaml), and the quote-stripping rule must be defined for both kinds. A alone can't strip quotes from YAML values because it doesn't know they came from YAML; B alone can't strip quotes at all because the stripping logic doesn't exist. A single integration test — read a quoted string from a YAML config file and expect it back unquoted — passes only when both sides are present and agree on that contract.
suggestion.interface_contract: In lib/ansible/config/manager.py: ensure_type(value, value_type, origin=None, origin_ftype=None) — a new origin_ftype keyword carrying the config file's type ('ini' or 'yaml'); unquoting of one outer quote pair applies to str/string values exactly when origin_ftype names a file type whose strings are quoted. And in get_config_value_and_origin: whenever a value is loaded from a config file, origin_ftype must be set to that file's type (A's gold patch already sets origin_ftype = ftype for both the ini and the yaml branch) and passed to both ensure_type call sites.
suggestion.taskA: INI string values are not unquoted correctly: since 2.15, 'ansible-config dump -c my.cfg' shows ANSIBLE_COW_PATH = "/usr/bin/cowsay" with literal quotes for values written quoted in the INI file. suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the server send the correct gRPC status codes (Canceled, DeadlineExceeded) when a request is canceled or times out. Task B, independently motivated, adds typed error helpers to the official Go SDK so SDK users can programmatically detect those conditions and write retry logic. The two only work together if they agree on the shared contract: the exact gRPC status codes on the wire. Server fixed but SDK has no helpers -> SDK users still can't detect timeouts; SDK has helpers but server still reports Internal -> the helpers report the wrong condition. Only both, agreeing on the codes, let an end-to-end test pass.
suggestion.interface_contract: The gRPC status code carried in the response: the server must return codes.Canceled for errors wrapping context.Canceled and codes.DeadlineExceeded for errors wrapping context.DeadlineExceeded (and keep NotFound/InvalidArgument/Unauthenticated for the existing error types); the SDK must expose classification helpers (e.g. IsCanceled(err), IsDeadlineExceeded(err), or typed errors) that inspect exactly those gRPC codes via the standard status package.
suggestion.taskA: Context cancellation and deadline exceeded errors are incorrectly classified as Internal/Unauthenticated in gRPC responses; the server must return Canceled and DeadlineExceeded for wrapped context errors while leaving all other behavior unchanged.
suggestion.taskB: The Go SDK (sdk/go) returns raw errors with no way for callers to distinguish failure kinds; SDK users implementing retry/backoff logic cannot tell a timeout or cancellation from a genuine server error. Add error classification helpers to the SDK that map gRPC status codes (NotFound, Unauthenticated, Canceled, DeadlineExceeded, Internal) into checkable typed errors or predicates.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A has value on its own for every consumer of the API (other-language clients, the HTTP gateway, monitoring/metrics dashboards) and is about server correctness, not the Go SDK. B has value on its own as client DX: even against a server that already returns perfect codes, SDK users today have no ergonomic way to branch on them. Neither ticket mentions the other; they meet only at the wire protocol.
suggestion.integration_point: The gRPC transport between the server's interceptor chain (internal/server/middleware/grpc ErrorUnaryInterceptor, internal/server/auth UnaryInterceptor) and the SDK client (sdk/go Transport over grpc.ClientConnInterface).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test: start a gRPC server wired with the real interceptor chain (or at least ErrorUnaryInterceptor) and a handler that surfaces ctx.Err() (e.g. returns fmt.Errorf('op: %w', ctx.Err()) once the context is done); call it through the SDK transport with a client deadline of a few milliseconds; assert the SDK's IsDeadlineExceeded(err) is true (and analogously for a canceled context). With A alone the SDK helper does not exist (test cannot pass/compile); with B alone the server returns Internal for the wrapped deadline error so the helper reports Internal; with both, agreeing on codes.DeadlineExceeded, the test passes.

notes: Contradictory is the weaker fit: the two tickets are semantically compatible (both map to codes.Canceled, no requirement contradicts the other), so the 'cannot both be true' bar is only met at the hunk level — both must rewrite the same classification block in ErrorUnaryInterceptor. If B's patch is written as a purely additive switch case, a naive git merge may actually succeed and the combined suite would pass, breaking the mutex soundness; the authoring step should write B as a rewrite of the whole block (e.g. dedup of the duplicated status.FromError check plus the ErrCanceled case) to force the collision. Alternative shared region: the error branch of auth.UnaryInterceptor in internal/server/auth/middleware.go (A inserts context checks there; a B ticket like 'distinguish token-not-found from malformed-token with distinct Unauthenticated messages' would edit the same branch) — viable but B feels more contrived there. For complementary, note sdk/go is largely generated code (protoc-gen-go-flipt-sdk), so B would realistically be a hand-written errors.go in sdk/go plus possibly a generator tweak; the e2e integration test needs the server side to actually emit a wrapped context error (auth path with a slow/canceled lookup, or a test handler), which is constructible but not free. Overall: contradictory ~2, complementary ~3 — plausible pairs grounded in real code structure, both needing authoring work to be sound.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the server honor a 'do not use the cache' instruction that a client can attach to a request (the Cache-Control: no-store header, which over gRPC arrives as a metadata entry named x-cache-control). Task B, filed by the SDK maintainer, adds a small helper to the Go SDK so SDK users can attach that same instruction to a single call (e.g. a NoStore(ctx) option). Neither side works alone: the server feature is useless to Go SDK users who have no way to send the directive, and the SDK helper is inert if the server ignores it. They must agree on the exact wire contract — metadata key x-cache-control, value no-store — and only then does an end-to-end test (read flag, update flag, read again with the helper, expect the fresh value) pass.
suggestion.interface_contract: Outgoing gRPC metadata key "x-cache-control" (grpc-gateway's runtime.MetadataPrefix "x-" + "cache-control") with value "no-store"; the server's CacheControlUnaryInterceptor treats exactly that key/value as the do-not-store mark for the request (and the HTTP gateway forwards the plain Cache-Control header into the same metadata key).
suggestion.taskA: Server-side: honor Cache-Control: no-store from clients (mark the request context, skip writing to the storage cache), and move flag caching into the storage layer so the cache actually reduces database load. Valuable on its own: any HTTP client (curl, the UI, other languages' SDKs) can already send the header, and storage-level flag caching helps regardless of the Go SDK.
suggestion.taskB: Go SDK (sdk/go): add a per-call helper, e.g. sdk.NoStore(ctx) returning a context, that attaches the no-store directive to the outgoing call, so SDK users who need the current state of a flag right after a change can force a fresh read without managing raw metadata keys themselves.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Different components, different owners: A is server behavior (internal/...), B is client ergonomics (sdk/go, a hand-written helper file alongside the generated code). A stands alone — the header contract is standard HTTP and usable by non-Go clients immediately. B reads as its own ticket ('SDK users have no way to request an uncached read') even though its usefulness is realized only once the server honors the directive, which is exactly the producer/consumer shape this family is meant to capture.
suggestion.integration_point: The SDK's outgoing metadata (sdk/go helper + authenticate/transport path in sdk/go) meets the server's CacheControlUnaryInterceptor in internal/server/middleware/grpc/middleware.go, which reads md.Get("x-cache-control") and calls cache.WithDoNotStore.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: In the cache-enabled integration suite (build/testing/integration, the existing cache harness with a short TTL): create a flag, read it once (populates cache), update the flag, then read again using the SDK's NoStore context — assert the updated value is returned immediately (before TTL expiry); a control read without the helper may still return the stale value. Fails with A alone (helper doesn't exist / directive never sent), fails with B alone (server ignores x-cache-control and serves the stale entry), passes only when both are present and agree on the key/value.

notes: Primary risk for the contradictory pair: B lives in the same subsystem as A, so a strict reviewer could call it 'the part of A that A didn't do' — mitigated by scoping B to rollouts/distributions (different methods, different motivation) rather than to flag caching. A second, weaker contradictory B was considered: an independent 'honor Cache-Control: no-cache' ticket that would create its own CacheControlUnaryInterceptor/constants in internal/server/middleware/grpc/middleware.go, colliding with A's identically-named symbols — real duplicate-definition conflict, but weaker independence since no-store and no-cache are two directives of the same header and would likely be filed together. For the complementary pair, note that sdk/go files are marked 'Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT', so B must be implemented as a small hand-written file (e.g. sdk/go/cache.go) — plausible but worth flagging to the authoring step. The complementary integration test requires the live-server dagger harness (cache suite), which already exists and was extended by A's test patch (FLIPT_CACHE_TTL=500ms), so it is feasible. Base-commit facts verified: internal/storage/cache/cache.go has only GetEvaluationRules cached with 3-arg set/get; the interceptor has GetFlag/UpdateFlag/DeleteFlag/variant invalidation cases that A removes; runtime.MetadataPrefix is 'x-'; the SDK has no header/metadata helper beyond the auth token.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Vuls keeps two separate, hand-maintained lists of 'which Ubuntu releases do we support'. One is the lifecycle/EOL date table (used to warn users when an OS is end-of-life); the other is the whitelist inside the Ubuntu security-API CVE detector (used to decide whether to fetch unfixed-CVE data for a host). At the base commit both lists stop before Ubuntu 22.04: the EOL table has no 22.04 entry, and the CVE detector's whitelist has no 2204/jammy entry. Task A fixes the EOL table; an independent Task B fixes the CVE detector's whitelist. A 22.04 host is only fully supported when BOTH lists agree that 22.04 exists — with only one fixed, the scan still breaks (either a bogus 'Failed to check EOL' warning, or the CVE detector silently skipping the host with 'Ubuntu 22.04 is not supported yet').

Note the two lists use different key formats ("22.04" vs "2204") and are maintained in different packages with no shared code — the contract is data-level agreement on the release set.

Add/correct the 20.04, 21.04, 21.10 and 22.04 entries in the Ubuntu lifecycle table.

Add "2110": "impish" and "2204": "jammy" to the supported-releases map in the GOST Ubuntu client.

The two lists are maintained independently and had already drifted (the EOL table contains 21.10 while the GOST whitelist does not). A's gold patch touches none of gost/, and A has full standalone value: correct EOL/ESM status for 20.04/22.04 regardless of whether GOST detection ever supports those releases. B likewise stands alone: enabling the Ubuntu API detector for jammy is valuable even if the EOL table is never updated.
suggestion.integration_point: The scan pipeline for an Ubuntu host: scanner.Scan → models.ScanResult.CheckEOL() → config.GetEOL (A's side), and detector.DetectCves → detectPkgsCvesWithGost → gost.Ubuntu.DetectCVEs → Ubuntu.supported (B's side). Both gate on the same ScanResult.Family/Release ("ubuntu"/"22.04").
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test, e.g. in the gost package (it already imports config, so no import cycle): for release 22.04, (1) call config.GetEOL(constant.Ubuntu, "22.04") and assert found==true and IsStandardSupportEnded(2022-05-01)==false, and (2) assert Ubuntu{}.supported("2204")==true (and "2110"). On the base commit it fails at (1); with only A's fix it fails at (2); with only B's fix it fails at (1); with both fixes it passes. A stronger variant runs models.ScanResult{Family:"ubuntu",Release:"22.04"}.CheckEOL() and asserts no 'Failed to check EOL' warning, combined with the supported() assertion.

notes: Real structure, not an invented split: gost/ubuntu.go's supported() map genuinely lags the config/os.go EOL table at the base commit (missing 2110/2204), and in vuls's actual history these lists were updated in separate PRs. Complementary confidence is 3 rather than 4 because the 'contract' is data-level agreement between two hardcoded lists in different packages (different key formats, no shared producer/consumer code path), and a strict reviewer might see B as 'the other half of 22.04 support' — though the motivations (lifecycle warnings vs CVE-detection coverage) and files are fully distinct. A's go.mod/go.sum dependency bumps (incl. the vulsio/gost library version) are incidental maintenance and not part of the behavioral fix. Contradictory family is weak: the only same-region collision (both tickets adding a "22.04" key to the same map literal, which would be a duplicate-key compile error if naively concatenated) requires B to be a subset of A's explicitly stated scope, failing the independence bar.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds a converter that turns Trivy scanner output into Vuls's standard scan-result JSON, and it deliberately keeps the identity fields the caller already put in (the server UUID and the format version). Task B, filed by a different developer, builds an uploader tool that takes a Vuls scan-result JSON on standard input, stamps it with a server UUID, and sends it to the FutureVuls SaaS backend. Each tool is useful on its own — A feeds Vuls's normal reporting/analysis, B centralizes any Vuls results — but the end-to-end workflow 'trivy | parser | uploader | SaaS' only works if both sides honor the same scan-result JSON contract: the parser must preserve/emit the fields (ServerUUID, JSONVersion, ScannedCves, Packages, LibraryScanners) that the uploader reads and forwards.
suggestion.interface_contract: The Vuls models.ScanResult JSON document: the parser's output must be a well-formed ScanResult that preserves the caller-supplied ServerUUID and JSONVersion (and populates ScannedCves/Packages/LibraryScanners), and the uploader must accept exactly that document on stdin, set/verify ServerUUID, and POST it (payload GroupID/Token/ScannedBy + the result body) to the SaaS URL, uploading the marshaled ScanResult to the returned S3 bucket/key.
suggestion.taskA: Provide a parser library (new Go package) that converts a Trivy vulnerability report JSON into a Vuls models.ScanResult: merge vulnerabilities by ID, distinguish OS-package results from library results, record confidence, affected packages, content, and sorted references, and preserve caller-supplied fields such as JSONVersion and ServerUUID.
suggestion.taskB: Provide a 'future-vuls upload' CLI that reads a Vuls scan-result JSON from stdin, takes --token/--url/--group-id/--uuid (with environment-variable fallbacks), performs the SaaS credential exchange, and uploads the result JSON to the S3 location returned by the backend.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is valuable even if B never existed: it lets any team run Trivy for scanning and Vuls for its normal reporting, diffing, and analysis on the converted results. B is valuable even if A never existed: it centralizes uploads of ordinary Vuls scan results to the SaaS backend. Neither ticket mentions the other; they are two ends of a pipeline that happen to meet on the pre-existing ScanResult format.
suggestion.integration_point: The parser's stdout (marshaled models.ScanResult JSON) piped into the uploader's stdin; both sides agree on the ScanResult schema and on ServerUUID/JSONVersion being carried through unchanged.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: Feed a Trivy report through the parser, pipe the resulting JSON into the uploader pointed at a mock SaaS HTTP server (returns a TempCredential and captures the S3 PutObject). Assert the uploaded S3 object equals the parsed ScanResult (with the supplied ServerUUID and JSONVersion intact) and that the request payload carried the correct GroupID/Token. The test fails with A alone (no uploader to receive the JSON) and with B alone (no JSON produced / no Trivy conversion), and passes only when both exist and agree on the contract.

notes: 1) The official patch bundles two unrelated features — the Trivy parser (A) and the SaaS uploader (B) — plus a SaasConf.GroupID int→int64 widening and go.mod bumps. This makes B feel like 'the other half of the PR' rather than a purely independent ticket, which caps the complementary confidence. 2) The shared contract (models.ScanResult JSON) is pre-existing in the repo, not introduced by A, so the coupling is shallower than a true producer/consumer pair. 3) A real gap: A's requirements explicitly forbid setting ScannedAt, but B's S3 key naming (renameKeyNameUTC) depends on ScannedAt; a zero ScannedAt yields a degenerate key. An authoring step would need to reconcile this (e.g., B falls back to the current time when ScannedAt is zero) for the integration test to be clean. 4) Contradictory is not viable: the two sides' file footprints are essentially disjoint (only additive go.mod/Makefile overlap), so no same-region collision or failing naive merge can be constructed. 5) The parser's OS-result branch in the gold patch does set ScannedAt, contradicting the stated requirement; the requirement text should be treated as the contract.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the command-line side: tctl splits --host into a list and puts every entry into a new ServerNames field on the database certificate signing request (keeping the old single ServerName field set to the first entry). Task B would be a separate, server-side ticket: the auth server's GenerateDatabaseCert currently copies only the single legacy ServerName into the certificate's SAN list, so even a request carrying many names gets a certificate with just one; B asks the server to put all names from the request into the certificate (and to keep working for old clients that only send the single name). Each ticket is worth doing on its own, but the end-to-end feature only works if both sides agree on the shared contract: the request carries the list in a field named ServerNames, and the server uses that list, falling back to the legacy single ServerName when the list is empty.
suggestion.interface_contract: proto.DatabaseCertRequest (api/client/proto/authservice.pb.go / authservice.proto): a repeated string field ServerNames (field number 4) carrying all SANs, plus the legacy string ServerName (field 2) holding the first entry. Server-side rule: certificate DNS names = ServerNames if non-empty, else [ServerName] if set. Client-side rule: ServerNames is always populated (even for a single host) and ServerName == ServerNames[0].
suggestion.taskA: tctl auth sign --format=db and --format=mongo should treat --host as a comma-separated list of hostnames/IPs: split it, put all entries in order into the new ServerNames field of the database cert request, set the subject CommonName to the first entry, keep the legacy ServerName field populated with the first entry for backward compatibility, and keep MongoDB Organization derived from the cluster name.
suggestion.taskB: The auth server's database certificate signing (lib/auth/db.go GenerateDatabaseCert) only ever puts the single legacy ServerName into the issued certificate's SAN list. A client that sends multiple server names in the request gets a certificate covering only one of them, so connections via the other hostnames/IPs fail TLS verification. The server should include every name the request carries in the certificate, and must keep accepting requests that only set the legacy single-name field (older tctl versions).
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone server-side bug ticket: the SAN-handling code in lib/auth/db.go is a real, separate component (the auth server) from the tctl CLI, and 'certificate only covers the first SAN' is a genuine defect an operator would report without knowing about the tctl work. A also has value beyond B: it fixes the CLI's inability to express multiple SANs at all, corrects the CommonName to the first entry, and preserves the legacy field for older servers. Caveat that caps confidence: B is the natural 'server half' of the same end-to-end feature A describes, so an author must frame B strictly around the server's existing single-SAN limitation (which predates A) to keep it from reading as a decomposition.
suggestion.integration_point: The DatabaseCertRequest message crossing the gRPC boundary: tctl's generateDatabaseKeysForKey (tool/tctl/common/auth_command.go) builds it, and Server.GenerateDatabaseCert (lib/auth/db.go) consumes req.ServerNames/req.ServerName to set tlsca.CertificateRequest.DNSNames.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test against a real auth server: (1) a request with ServerNames=[a.example.com, b.example.com, 192.168.1.1] yields a certificate whose SANs contain all of them (fails on base: server only reads ServerName; fails with A alone: client sets ServerNames but server ignores it; fails with B alone: client never populates ServerNames); (2) a legacy request with only ServerName=c.example.com still yields a cert with that SAN (the fallback contract). Both pass only when the client and server changes agree on the field name and the fallback rule.

notes: Base state verified: lib/auth/db.go GenerateDatabaseCert sets certReq.DNSNames = []string{req.ServerName} only when ServerName != ''; the DatabaseCertRequest struct has just CSR/ServerName/TTL (no ServerNames); tctl's generateDatabaseKeysForKey sets CommonName = a.genHost and ServerName = a.genHost. The gold patch is client-side + proto only; the server never learns to read ServerNames, which is exactly why the complementary pair is the natural fit here. A's fail-to-pass list includes unrelated tests (TestCheckKubeCluster, TestTrimDurationSuffix, TestDatabaseServerResource, TestAuthSignKubeconfig) that only fail on base because the modified test file (auth_command_test.go) must compile for the whole package — an authoring note, not a signal of extra scope. Contradictory family is weak: the only same-region collisions (dropping the legacy ServerName population, or changing MongoDB Organization to the host domain) are direct counter-demands to A's explicit requirements, so B would not read as an independent ticket. Complementary confidence is 3 rather than 4 because B is genuinely the server-side half of A's feature and needs careful framing to stay independent.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the producer side: the Touch ID library gains a diagnostics function that reports, in one result, whether the binary is signed, has the right entitlements, passed the platform policy test and the Secure Enclave test, and whether Touch ID is therefore usable. Task B is a separate consumer ticket in the CLI: today 'tsh mfa add' silently hides the Touch ID device option whenever Touch ID is unavailable, so users on broken machines have no idea why; B asks that the specific reason (e.g. 'binary is not signed', 'missing keychain entitlements', 'Secure Enclave test failed') be shown to the user. The two only work together if they agree on the shape of the diagnostic result — the Diag() function and its named fields — which A defines and B consumes.
suggestion.interface_contract: touchid.Diag() (*DiagResult, error) in lib/auth/touchid, where DiagResult has exactly the bool fields HasCompileSupport, HasSignature, HasEntitlements, PassedLAPolicyTest, PassedSecureEnclaveTest, IsAvailable; B's CLI code maps the false fields to human-readable reasons and must treat IsAvailable as the gate for whether any reason is shown.
suggestion.taskA: Enhanced Touch ID availability and diagnostics: availability in tsh is currently compile-time-only and produces false positives for unsigned/unentitled binaries or machines without Touch ID; derive availability from a diagnostics check (signature, entitlements, LA policy test, Secure Enclave test) exposed as DiagResult/Diag(), and keep registration and login working through the new path.
suggestion.taskB: tsh mfa add silently drops the TOUCHID device type when Touch ID is unavailable, with no explanation. When the TOUCHID option is hidden from the device-type list/prompt, print the concrete reason(s) taken from the Touch ID diagnostics (unsigned binary, missing keychain-access-groups entitlement, failed platform policy test, failed Secure Enclave test) so users can self-diagnose instead of filing support tickets.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B lives in a different file (tool/tsh/mfa.go, initWebDevs/device-type prompt) and serves a different user story (registering an MFA device and understanding why Touch ID is not offered) than A (correctness of the availability signal plus the touchid diag command). A is fully valuable without B — it fixes false-positive availability and ships a diagnostics command mirroring the existing 'tsh fido2 diag'. B is not 'the other half of A': A's patch does not touch mfa.go, and A's ticket is complete without any mfa UX change. B is a natural follow-up consumer of A's new API, which is exactly the producer/consumer relationship this family requires.
suggestion.integration_point: tool/tsh/mfa.go: initWebDevs() (line ~65) and the device-type prompt path (deviceTypesFromSecondFactor / mfaAddCommand.run) call touchid.Diag() and render per-field reasons when IsAvailable is false.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One integration test (in tool/tsh, against a small extracted helper like touchIDUnavailableReasons(diag *touchid.DiagResult) []string so it is testable without a real TTY): stub the native layer via the exported touchid.Native with a fake whose Diag() returns IsAvailable=false, HasSignature=false, HasEntitlements=true, PassedLAPolicyTest=true, PassedSecureEnclaveTest=true; assert the reason list contains the 'not signed' message and that the mfa device-type list omits TOUCHID. Fails with A alone (no reason is surfaced in mfa add), fails with B alone (touchid.Diag/DiagResult do not exist in the base library, so B's code does not compile), passes with both agreeing on the DiagResult field names/semantics.

notes: Task A's gold patch is a bundle of three things: (1) the library diagnostics API, (2) a 'tsh touchid diag' CLI command that stays registered even when Touch ID is unavailable (tool/tsh/touchid.go, and presumably tool/tsh/tsh.go in the truncated portion), and (3) macOS 10.12 compatibility (Info.plist LSMinimumSystemVersion, -mmacosx-version-min=10.12 cgo flag, kSecAccessControlTouchIDAny in register.m). Because of (2) and (3), the two most 'obvious' independent B candidates — a touchid diag command and a lower-minimum-macOS ticket — are already inside A, i.e. decompositions, so the contradictory family is weak (the only genuinely independent collision, caching IsAvailable, is unmotivated since the base native check is a constant). The complementary family via the mfa-add explanation is the best fit: real shared interface (DiagResult fields are fixed by A's requirements), independent motivation, and a constructible single integration test. Caveats keeping it at confidence 3: tool/tsh has no existing test files, so B's tests need an extracted pure helper; and B's motivation presupposes that diagnostic reasons exist, which only A provides — acceptable under the producer/consumer definition since A stands on its own, but it is the main thing a later authoring step should sanity-check. Also note the base test file lib/auth/touchid/api_test.go (fakeNative with IsAvailable) is rewritten by A's test patch, so any B-side tests must not depend on the old interface shape.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the proxy's authentication step report the true *kind* of failure: a real 'you are not allowed' versus a plumbing problem like 'that Kubernetes cluster is not registered here' or 'no tunnel to the remote cluster'. Task B, from a different developer, makes the proxy *speak Kubernetes* on errors: instead of replying with Teleport's internal JSON, it replies with a standard Kubernetes Status object (the format kubectl parses) whose embedded code matches the error kind. Neither alone gives the user experience 'kubectl shows a 403 with a real message when forbidden, and a 400 with the real message when the cluster is unregistered'. They must agree on one contract: the error kind produced by authenticate must survive untouched all the way to the response formatter, which maps it to the Status code.
suggestion.interface_contract: The error returned by Forwarder.authenticate/authorize must carry its trace error kind (AccessDenied -> 403, BadParameter -> 400, NotFound -> 404, ConnectionProblem -> 504, other -> 500) through the withAuth/withAuthStd handlers into the HTTP response, and the response must be a Kubernetes metav1.Status JSON object (Status: Failure, Message: user-facing error text, Code: the mapped code) written with HTTP 500 as the outer status, which is the only outer code kubectl parses the Status body for.
suggestion.taskA: Authentication failures in the Kubernetes proxy are indistinguishable: every failure while establishing a request's identity is reported as the same 'access denied' error. Fix authenticate so that genuine authorization rejections are AccessDenied (trace.IsAccessDenied true) while non-authorization failures — the requested Kubernetes cluster not being registered locally, or no reverse tunnel to reach a remote Teleport cluster — keep their original error kind (trace.IsAccessDenied false).
suggestion.taskB: kubectl users see opaque Teleport JSON when the proxy rejects or fails a request, and kubectl cannot parse the failure into a proper Kubernetes error (no Status object, no meaningful code). Make the kube proxy render all handler errors — auth failures, authorization failures, and forwarding errors — as standard Kubernetes Status objects with the correct embedded code, so clients see e.g. Forbidden with the real message instead of a 500 with internal JSON.
suggestion.independence_rationale: Each ticket is motivated by a distinct user pain: A is about error *classification* (operators/clients cannot tell 'denied' from 'misconfigured/unreachable'); B is about error *presentation* (kubectl cannot parse the response at all). A has value even if B never existed: the classified error kind is what audit logs, metrics, and any future consumer (including B's formatter) rely on, and TestAuthenticate validates it directly. B has value even if A never existed: it would still convert every error into a parseable Status object (just with wrong codes for non-auth failures). The coupling is that B's correct codes depend on A's correct kinds — a real shared contract, not a decomposition, though the two were historically shipped in one upstream PR, which is why independence is only moderate.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/kube/proxy/forwarder.go: the withAuth/withAuthStd wrappers (where authenticate's error is returned to the handler) and the response formatting path (the custom error writer used by those wrappers, plus the forward.ErrorHandler on the oxy forwarders used by catchAll/exec/portForward).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test driving the proxy end-to-end (or the withAuth handler with a mocked auth client): (1) a request whose certificate names an unregistered Kubernetes cluster must yield a Kubernetes Status object with Code 400 and a message containing 'not registered' (outer HTTP 500, body parseable as metav1.Status); (2) a request the user is genuinely forbidden for must yield Status Code 403 with the access-denied message. Base code fails both: (1) comes back as 403 in Teleport JSON, (2) as Teleport JSON. A alone fails (1)/(2) on format (no Status object). B alone fails (1) on code (403 instead of 400, because authenticate still reclassifies everything as AccessDenied). Both together pass.

notes: Key structural facts verified at the base commit: (1) Forwarder.authenticate (lib/kube/proxy/forwarder.go ~line 360) wraps ALL setupContext errors in trace.AccessDenied; setupContext returns trace.BadParameter for 'no reverse tunnel' (line 446) and CheckOrSetKubeCluster (lib/kube/utils/utils.go:177) returns trace.BadParameter for an unregistered cluster and trace.NotFound when none are registered — these are the non-auth failures A must preserve. (2) The unknown-cluster error in authorize() (line 564) is a separate function A does not touch, so it is not a collision site. (3) httplib.MakeHandler/MakeStdHandler hardcode trace.WriteError; A's new *WithErrorWriter variants are additive, so the httplib half of A cannot contradict anything. (4) The kube client side already parses metav1.Status from non-101 responses (roundtrip.go NewConnection, lines 207-231), which is exactly the format B's server-side writer must emit — a genuine pre-existing contract on the wire. (5) The integration/ directory's KubeSuite is gated behind an env var and a real kubeconfig, so the complementary integration test would most naturally live as a unit-level test of the withAuth handler with mocks (as TestAuthenticate does). Caveat: A and B were one upstream PR, so the 'two developers' framing is constructed; the contract (error kind preserved to the Status code) is real and testable, hence complementary viable at confidence 3 rather than higher. Contradictory family is weak: no independently-motivated B forces incompatible edits to A's exact lines.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds a shared, reusable table builder that fits output to the terminal width (the 'producer' of a new layout API). Task B is a separate ticket about a different command: 'tsh request ls' prints access requests with a Roles column that can be very long and overflows narrow terminals, so it should render its table through that shared builder with Roles as the truncation column (the 'consumer'). Neither ticket mentions the other; each is worth doing alone. The single integration test — a request table with a long roles list comes out within 80 columns with the roles cell cut and ending in '...' — passes only when A's builder exists AND B's code calls it.
suggestion.interface_contract: func MakeTableWithTruncatedColumn(columnOrder []string, rows [][]string, truncatedColumn string) asciitable.Table in lib/asciitable: the named column takes the leftover terminal width (80 fallback when size unknown), its oversized cells are cut and end with '...', other columns are capped proportionally to terminal width. B's ticket must pin this exact name/signature so the two agents agree.
suggestion.taskA: Add the shared terminal-width-fitting table builder to lib/asciitable (as above) and convert the tsh node/application/database listings and the tctl text listings to use it, replacing tsh's private copy of the layout.
suggestion.taskB: tsh request ls overflows narrow terminals because the Roles column joins many role names into one long cell. Render the request listing so the Roles column absorbs the leftover terminal width and is cut with '...' when it does not fit, using the shared truncated-column table builder from lib/asciitable.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A fixes tsh ls and tctl get and creates a reusable layout API — valuable even if no other command ever uses it. B fixes a different command (tsh request ls, in tool/tsh/access_request.go, which A never touches) with different columns (ID, User, Roles, Created, Status) and its own readability motivation for people reviewing access requests. B is not 'the rest of A': A's ticket scopes itself to the node/app/database listings, and request ls was simply not converted.
suggestion.integration_point: tool/tsh/access_request.go showRequestTable: it must call asciitable.MakeTableWithTruncatedColumn (defined by A in lib/asciitable/table.go) instead of asciitable.MakeTable.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: A test that runs showRequestTable (or its table construction) with a request carrying a long comma-joined roles list, capturing output to a buffer: assert every line is <= 80 chars (terminal size unavailable in tests, so the 80 fallback applies) and the roles cell ends with '...'. With A alone the test fails (showRequestTable still uses MakeTable, full-width roles). With B alone it fails to compile (the builder does not exist). With both, agreeing on the builder's name and semantics, it passes.

notes: Two cautions. (1) The most tempting contradictory B — 'show the app's Teleport version in tctl get apps' — is a decomposition of A: A's gold patch already adds the Version column to appCollection.writeText and the GetTeleportVersion() method on the Application interface precisely for that, so it was rejected in favor of the database Type column, which A does not touch. (2) A's app.go change (GetTeleportVersion on the Application interface) is a small auxiliary piece; adding another method to that same interface would be a weak conflict because additive interface changes merge cleanly. The complementary family's soundness hinges on B's ticket naming the shared builder's exact signature; if B were free to write its own private helper (as tsh originally did), B alone would pass and the seed would break — the ticket text must pin the contract. Both families are rated 3: real, precise shared structure, but each needs careful ticket wording to stay sound and independent.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A makes the config *writer*: 'teleport db configure create' now emits aws/ad/gcp/tls sections into the generated database agent YAML. An independent task B makes the config *reader*: 'teleport db configure bootstrap' (the AWS IAM policy generator in lib/configurators/databases/aws.go) currently decides whether an agent needs Redshift/ElastiCache/MemoryDB permissions only by pattern-matching the database URI against standard AWS endpoint hostnames. For a static database behind a custom endpoint, alias, or proxy, it generates no permissions at all; B would make it also look at the 'aws' section of each configured database (region, redshift.cluster_id, elasticache.replication_group_id, memorydb.cluster_name, secret_store). Neither side alone is useful for the end-to-end flow: A's generated file carries the metadata but the base bootstrap ignores it; B's new detection logic finds nothing in files generated by the base 'db configure create'. Only when both exist and agree on the aws-section schema does the pipeline 'generate config -> bootstrap IAM policy' work.
suggestion.interface_contract: The 'aws' sub-section of each db_service.databases[] entry in the agent YAML — 'region', 'redshift.cluster_id', 'elasticache.replication_group_id', 'memorydb.cluster_name', 'secret_store.{key_prefix,kms_key_id}' — as parsed by the existing config.Database.AWS struct in lib/config/fileconf.go (DatabaseAWS, lines ~1246-1285). A renders it from DatabaseSampleFlags in the databaseAgentConfigurationTemplate; B consumes it in hasRedshiftDatabases/hasElastiCacheDatabases/hasMemoryDBDatabases and buildPolicyDocument/buildPolicyBoundaryDocument in lib/configurators/databases/aws.go.
suggestion.taskA: Support additional database configuration flags in 'teleport db configure create' (TLS ca_cert_file, aws-region, aws-redshift-cluster-id, ad-domain, ad-spn, ad-keytab-file, gcp-project-id, gcp-instance-id), rendering the matching tls/aws/ad/gcp sections in the generated config; rename db start's --ca-cert to --ca-cert-file.
suggestion.taskB: 'db configure bootstrap' misses static AWS databases whose URI does not match the standard AWS endpoint pattern (custom domains, aliases, proxy front-ends): the generated IAM policy omits redshift/elasticache/memorydb statements even though the database config declares an 'aws' section. The bootstrap should treat the 'aws' section of a static database (region plus redshift.cluster_id / elasticache.replication_group_id / memorydb.cluster_name / secret_store) as a first-class signal for which permissions to grant, not just URI shape.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A is a CLI-ergonomics ticket for config generation and is fully valuable on its own — users of 'db start' and hand-edited configs get the rendered sections regardless of B. B is a correctness/coverage ticket for the IAM bootstrap tool, motivated by deployments where URIs are not canonical AWS endpoints; it never needs to mention A and works on hand-written config files too. They meet only at the pre-existing YAML schema (config.Database.AWS), which is the natural shared contract.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/configurators/databases/aws.go buildPolicyDocument/buildPolicyBoundaryDocument consuming a config produced by config.MakeDatabaseAgentConfigString (lib/config/database.go) and parsed via config.ReadConfig (lib/config/fileconf.go).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One test: build DatabaseSampleFlags for a static Redshift database with a deliberately non-canonical URI (e.g. redshift.example.com:5439) plus DatabaseAWSRegion and DatabaseAWSRedshiftClusterID, call MakeDatabaseAgentConfigString, parse with ReadConfig, run NewAWSConfigurator (Manual mode) and assert the policy contains redshift:DescribeClusters (and boundary redshift:GetClusterCredentials) statements. Fails with A alone (base bootstrap only URI-matches), fails with B alone (base generator emits no aws section), passes with both.

notes: Base code facts that support the analysis: (1) config.Database in lib/config/fileconf.go already has TLS, AWS (incl. Redshift/ElastiCache/MemoryDB/SecretStore), GCP and AD fields, and ReadConfig uses yaml.UnmarshalStrict — so the reader-side schema A emits into already exists and is strict (a generated file with unknown keys would fail to parse, which is why A's template keys must match exactly). (2) The base template has a latent bug: the dynamic_labels block is gated by a second '{{- if .StaticDatabaseStaticLabels }}' instead of a dynamic-labels condition (lib/config/database.go ~line 128), so an independent 'fix dynamic labels' ticket would touch the same template region as A but its one-line fix composes cleanly with A's insertions — again not a mutex. (3) The fail_to_pass list includes TestDatabaseConfig and TestDatabaseCLIFlags in lib/config/configuration_test.go even though the visible test patch only edits lib/config/database_test.go; the full PR's test patch presumably also extends those cases, but the pairing analysis is unaffected. suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds a bulk import pipeline for ISBNdb data dumps: it reads each line, filters out non-books, and queues the results into the import queue marked with the status 'staged' (i.e. 'queued but not ready to import yet'). suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the plumbing: two small helper functions that answer 'does this user have a pending email confirmation?' and 'wipe that pending confirmation cleanly.' Task B is a separate, genuinely useful admin feature that needs exactly those two answers: on the admin user-management screen, show whether each selected user has a stuck pending confirmation and give the admin a button to clear it so the user can receive a fresh email. Neither task is useful without the other's contract — A's helpers are pointless if nothing consumes them centrally, and B cannot be built correctly without a single authoritative way to read/clear the pending state. They must agree on the helper API (names, arguments, and the meaning of 'pending'), and only when both are present does an end-to-end admin flow test pass.
suggestion.interface_contract: The centralized validation-state API on the user email module: user.email.isValidationPending(uid, email?) -> Promise<boolean> (true only while a pending confirmation exists for that user, case-insensitive email match when an email is given) and user.email.expireValidation(uid) -> Promise<void> (removes the pending reference and its confirmation object so a subsequent non-forced sendValidationEmail is accepted). B must read and clear pending state only through these two helpers, never through the legacy raw database key.
suggestion.taskA: Centralize email validation state management: introduce isValidationPending and expireValidation and migrate validation-email sending, profile email updates, password-reset completion, email confirmation, and header rendering to use them, removing inconsistent direct access to the legacy per-user flag.
suggestion.taskB: Admin tooling for stuck email confirmations: add an admin action (socket/API + UI on the manage-users screen) that, for selected users, reports whether an email confirmation is currently pending and lets the admin expire/clear it so a new confirmation email can be sent — motivated by support tickets from users who changed devices and can never re-trigger the confirmation email.
suggestion.independence_rationale: A has clear standalone value: it fixes real inconsistency across five call sites and is the kind of refactor a maintainer files on its own. B is a believable, separate feature request (admins need to unstick users' email confirmation) that a different developer would file without reference to A. B is not 'the other half' of A — it is a new consumer of the capability A centralizes. The main caveat keeping this at a 2 rather than higher: B could technically be written against the legacy raw key instead of A's helpers, in which case the two would not actually agree on a contract, so the integration test must specifically require the helper-based path.
suggestion.integration_point: The new admin action in src/socket.io/admin (user/email area) calls user.email.isValidationPending(uid) to populate the 'pending' flag and user.email.expireValidation(uid) to clear it; this is the single place A's producer helpers and B's consumer feature meet.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One end-to-end test: create a user, trigger a pending confirmation, call the new admin 'show pending' action and assert it reports pending=true; call the admin 'clear/expire' action; assert the report is now pending=false AND that a subsequent non-forced sendValidationEmail succeeds (proving the clear went through the centralized helper, not just a UI flag). This passes only when A's helpers exist with the agreed semantics and B's admin action routes through them; with A absent (B using the raw key) or B absent (no admin action), the test fails.

notes: The codebase at the base commit confirms the structure A relies on: the legacy key uid:{uid}:confirm:email:sent is read/written in src/user/email.js (sendValidationEmail, confirmByUid), src/middleware/header.js (isEmailConfirmSent), src/user/profile.js (updateEmail), and src/user/reset.js (commit), and the confirm:{code} object stores {email, uid}. There is no existing confirm:byUid reference key or isValidationPending/expireValidation helper at base, so A is genuinely introducing the centralized contract. The strongest pairing is complementary (A = producer of the helper contract, B = an independent admin consumer), but it is only a 2 because B could be authored against the legacy key and thus fail to actually depend on A's interface — the integration test must force the helper path. A contradictory seed is imaginable (B = fix the resend cooldown by keeping the confirmation object and computing elapsed time, colliding with A's expireValidation-deletes-object semantics in the same sendValidationEmail block) but it requires B to be deliberately written to avoid A's helpers, so it reads more like an adversarial rewrite than a natural independent ticket; scored low. A subtle A-internal note for the authoring step: the gold patch's isValidationPending compares the supplied email to confirmObj.email without lowercasing the supplied value, while the requirement asks for case-insensitive matching — the authoring step should make the helper normalize both sides so the 'updatedemail@me.com matches updatedEmail@me.com' test is robust.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the 'brain' of email confirmation: a library method canSendValidation(uid, email) that answers 'may a confirmation email be sent right now?' based on whether one is pending and how long ago it was sent. Task B, a separate ticket about the user-facing email-change flow, needs exactly that answer: when a user opens the edit-email page and submits the same (or any) address, the flow currently always sends a fresh confirmation email, producing duplicate mail and never telling the user to wait. B's fix is to consult the resend gate before sending and surface the 'already sent, wait N minutes' error. Neither task alone makes the integration scenario work: without A the gate does not exist; without B the email-change flow never asks the gate.
suggestion.interface_contract: user.email.canSendValidation(uid, email) -> Promise<boolean>: true when no confirmation is pending for the user, or the pending one's remaining lifetime indicates the configured resend interval (emailConfirmInterval minutes) has elapsed; false otherwise. B must call it before sending from the email-change interstitial and treat false as 'block + show confirm-email-already-sent error'.
suggestion.taskA: Email confirmation expiry and resend consistency (the original ticket): strict-boolean isValidationPending, getValidationExpiry exposing the pending record's remaining TTL, registered emailConfirmExpiry default, and canSendValidation implementing the resend interval.
suggestion.taskB: Email change flow spams duplicate confirmation emails: when a logged-in user changes their email (account edit interstitial), a confirmation email is sent unconditionally, even if one was sent minutes ago; the user gets duplicate mail and the 'please wait N minutes' message is unreachable. Fix the interstitial to check resend eligibility before sending and show the wait error when not eligible.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as its own ticket (duplicate email sends / missing wait message in the edit-email flow) and A has standalone value (correct library semantics, expiry config, admin API correctness). Caveat: A's actual gold patch already contains the interstitial fix, so B overlaps A's real scope — this pair is closer to splitting one upstream fix into library vs. flow, which caps the independence signal.
suggestion.integration_point: src/user/interstitials.js — Interstitials.email callback, where sendValidationEmail is invoked for email changes; it must consult user.email.canSendValidation (defined in src/user/email.js by A) before sending.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: Integration test: (1) create a user with an unconfirmed email; (2) trigger a pending confirmation (sendValidationEmail); (3) submit the email-change interstitial with the same address; (4) assert the interstitial surfaces 'confirm-email-already-sent' (or sends no new confirmation) instead of always sending. Fails with A alone (interstitial never checks the gate) and with B alone (canSendValidation undefined / no expiry semantics), passes only when both agree on the contract.

notes: Base-commit facts: confirm:byUid:<uid> TTL = emailConfirmInterval minutes (10) and confirm:<code> TTL = hard-coded 24h; emailConfirmExpiry does not exist in install/data/defaults.json; isValidationPending returns non-strict values; canSendValidation/getValidationExpiry do not exist. Callers of sendValidationEmail: socket user.emailConfirm (removed by A), admin bulk (force:true), admin email test (force:1), user.create welcome email, profile updateEmail (force:1), interstitial (force:true). The strongest contradictory candidate (configurable link expiry) is a decomposition of A; the truly independent admin bulk-send fix (add force:true in src/socket.io/admin/user.js) composes with A without collision, so no mutex seed is sound. Complementary is viable but weak (confidence 2) because A's gold patch already implements B's interstitial change, making B 'the part of A that A didn't do' from a pure-library perspective; a later authoring step would need to scope A down to the library/config surface (src/user/email.js + defaults.json + admin templates) and keep the interstitial fix exclusively in B to make the pair sound.
