Task B is a separate display ticket: 'ansible-doc -t role -l only shows the role name, entry point and a short blurb; show the role's description column too.' B is a consumer of the summary dict that A produces. The two must agree on the contract that every role summary dict carries a 'description' key; only when A (producer) and B (consumer) are both present does a listing of a role with no metadata show the literal text UNDOCUMENTED.
suggestion.interface_contract: The role summary dict produced by RoleMixin._build_summary() (and returned by _create_role_list()): keys 'collection', 'entry_points' (name -> short description) and, after A, 'description' (str; 'UNDOCUMENTED' when the role provides no galaxy_info metadata). B's display code reads summary['description'] for each role in the -t role -l output.
suggestion.taskA: Same as the original ticket: no-color markup delimiters in ansible-doc plus _build_summary(role, collection, meta, argspec) that always includes a 'description' field ('UNDOCUMENTED' when meta/galaxy_info is absent) while preserving 'collection' and 'entry_points'.
suggestion.taskB: ansible-doc -t role -l output is too terse: it prints role name, entry point and the entry point's short description, but nothing about the role itself. Add the role's description to the listing output (a new column), sourced from the role summary data. (No mention of markup rendering or of where the description value comes from.)

However, A's value here is only partially independent of B — the 'description'/'UNDOCUMENTED' half of A exists mainly to feed B's new column, which is why this pairing is weaker than the contradictory one; the markup half of A is fully independent.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/ansible/cli/doc.py: _build_summary() (A, produces the dict) feeds _create_role_list() -> DocCLI._display_available_roles() (B, renders the listing rows).
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: A unit/integration test that builds a role summary for a role whose meta has no galaxy_info (A's code) and then renders the listing with B's _display_available_roles change, asserting the output row contains 'UNDOCUMENTED'. A alone: no description key to display (or B's column absent) -> fails. B alone on base code: summary has no 'description' -> column empty/missing -> fails. Both together, agreeing on the key -> passes.

notes: The strongest collision region is DocCLI.tty_ify in lib/ansible/cli/doc.py: it is a compact, single-purpose function whose per-markup lines are exactly what A rewrites (no-color delimiters; the gold patch restructures it around a NOCOLOR/STYLE table and stringc), and a color-emphasis ticket for C() is a natural, independently-motivated B that must edit the same line. Caveat that keeps contradictory at 4 rather than 5: B is in the same feature family as A (the real gold patch already implements color-aware markup rendering), so a strict reviewer might see B as anticipating A's direction; the independence rests on B being scoped to color-ON emphasis only. The role-summary half of A is a poor site for an independent B: A rewrites _load_argspec/_build_summary/_create_role_list/_create_role_doc/_find_all_normal_roles together (new _load_role_data/_load_metadata, 3-tuple role entries, error propagation), so any B touching that region (e.g. 'show role description in -t role -l') is either a decomposition of A or only weakly complementary (the summary dict contract is real, but B's display change lives in a different function than A's producer change). The tty_ify-based contradictory pair is the recommendation; the complementary pair is included as a secondary, lower-confidence option. suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the producer side: the shared URL helper (fetch_url / Request.open) learns to transparently decode gzip responses and to expose a decompress switch. A second, independently-motivated ticket B would be the consumer side: make the uri module correctly handle gzip-encoded responses — parse the JSON body when the payload is auto-decompressed, and leave the body un-parsed (no json key) when the user opts out with decompress=false. Each is worth doing on its own (A fixes every module that downloads over HTTP; B gives uri users a working json result and an opt-out for gzip endpoints), but only when BOTH are present and agree on the contract does the end-to-end uri-gzip integration test pass.
suggestion.interface_contract: fetch_url(module, url, ..., decompress=True) returns (response, info) where, when the server sent Content-Encoding: gzip and decompress is True, response.read() yields the DECODED bytes (and info still carries the original content-encoding header); when decompress is False, response.read() yields the raw compressed bytes. The uri module must call fetch_url with decompress taken from its own new decompress parameter and must only attempt JSON parsing of the returned body.
suggestion.taskA: Gzip-encoded HTTP responses are not handled: add transparent gzip decompression to ansible.module_utils.urls (GzipDecodedReader, a decompress flag defaulting to True threaded through Request.open/open_url/fetch_url/fetch_file, HAS_GZIP, MissingModuleError.module) so callers receive decoded content.
suggestion.taskB: The uri module mis-handles gzip-encoded responses: add a decompress option to uri and make it return a parsed json result for auto-decompressed gzip responses, while (with decompress=false) returning the raw payload and no json key, so users can hit gzip endpoints either way.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B reads as its own user-facing ticket (uri users getting json out of a gzip endpoint / an opt-out), and A has value on its own (every HTTP-downloading module benefits from correct decompression, and get_url is fixed by A alone). However, independence is WEAK: the original problem statement already lists 'uri should expose decompress and pass it through' as one of A's requirements, so B is really the module-level surface of the same feature rather than a separately-filed ticket. It is best viewed as a decomposition of A into core-vs-module layers.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/ansible/modules/uri.py — the uri() helper's fetch_url(...) call (gains decompress=...) and main()'s body/JSON handling (parse_content_type + r.read() + json.loads), meeting A's fetch_url/Request.open decompression in lib/ansible/module_utils/urls.py.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: One integration test (mirroring test/integration/targets/uri/tasks/main.yml): (1) uri against a gzip endpoint with default decompress → assert result.json is parsed (gzipped truthy); (2) uri with decompress=false → assert result.json is undefined. A alone fails (2) because uri has no decompress knob to disable decoding; B alone fails (1) because without A's core decompression the body is still gzip bytes and json parsing fails; both together, agreeing on the fetch_url(decompress=...) contract, pass.

notes: This task is a single cohesive feature (gzip decompression) whose official scope already spans the core module_utils AND the uri/get_url modules — the problem statement explicitly requires uri and get_url to expose decompress. That makes a clean independent pair hard: any complementary B (uri/get_url gzip handling) is a slice of A (decomposition, hence low confidence), and any contradictory B has to be contrived because A's edits (new gzip block at the tail of Request.open, new kwargs on open_url/fetch_url/fetch_file, MissingModuleError.module) are additive and merge cleanly with neighboring changes. The most defensible reading is complementary at confidence 2 (producer=core fetch_url decompression, consumer=uri module), with the caveat that it is largely a decomposition of A's own module-level requirements rather than two genuinely separate tickets. Contradictory is not viable at a soundness level.

suggestion.simple_explanation: Task A builds the plumbing: the base error class carries the originating YAML node on a public `obj` attribute, and the vault decryption entry points accept an optional `obj` argument and attach it to the error they raise. Task B is a separate, user-facing ticket: when a config file (e.g. ansible.cfg in YAML form) contains a vault-encrypted value that cannot be decrypted, the failure should point at the file and line of that value. B's side of the deal is making the encrypted-scalar object hand itself (and its recorded position) to the decrypt call when its plaintext is requested. Only when both sides exist does the error carry the location; each side alone is inert.
suggestion.interface_contract: VaultLib.decrypt(vaulttext, filename=None, obj=None) and VaultLib.decrypt_and_get_vault_id(vaulttext, filename=None, obj=None): the optional obj names the originating YAML node, and any AnsibleVaultFormatError raised must have its public `obj` attribute set to the caller-supplied value; correspondingly, AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode.data must invoke self.vault.decrypt(self._ciphertext, obj=self) so the scalar itself travels with the call.
suggestion.taskA: Expose and preserve the originating YAML object on Ansible errors (public `obj`, lazily rendered extended position details, settable message, re-raise-with-obj in task loading) and extend the vault decrypt entry points to accept and forward `obj` onto raised format errors.
suggestion.taskB: Config-manager vault error locality: reading a vaulted value from a YAML config file that fails to decrypt currently produces 'There was a vault format error' with no idea where the value lives. Make the single-value encrypted scalar pass itself to the vault decrypt call (and have the vault library accept it) so the surfaced error can name the config file and line of the offending value.
suggestion.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone UX ticket (bad vaulted config value -> unactionable error) with its own user story. A is useful on its own: the public obj/lazy-message error API and the task-loading re-raise behavior fix playbook parse errors independent of config files. The weakness: A's problem statement already explicitly scopes 'the vault decryption entry points ... should be able to receive the originating YAML node', and A's own test requires data to pass obj=self, so B's code change overlaps heavily with A's — B reads partly as 'the config-manager half of A' rather than a fully separate ticket.
suggestion.integration_point: lib/ansible/parsing/yaml/objects.py AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode.data (producer side, calls vault.decrypt) meeting lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py VaultLib.decrypt/decrypt_and_get_vault_id (consumer side, accepts obj and sets exc.obj); surfaced end-to-end through lib/ansible/config/manager.py ensure_type/_loop_entries when a config value is a vaulted scalar.
suggestion.integration_test_sketch: A single test that (1) attaches a mock vault whose decrypt records its arguments to an AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode and asserts the recorded obj is the scalar itself when .data is read, and (2) runs the real VaultLib.decrypt on a malformed vault envelope with an obj sentinel and asserts the raised AnsibleVaultFormatError.obj is the sentinel. It fails on base (decrypt has no obj param / data passes nothing), fails with only A's error-API changes if the data/decrypt wiring is absent, and fails with only B's data-side change if decrypt does not accept obj (TypeError) — passing only when both sides agree on the contract.

notes: Base-commit verification: AnsibleError.__init__ stores _obj and computes self.message eagerly (errors/__init__.py:53-71); task.py:224 and helpers.py:126 read e._obj; objects.py:120 data calls self.vault.decrypt(self._ciphertext) with no obj; vault __init__.py:652/666 decrypt signatures lack obj; constructor.py:112-114 never sets ansible_pos on AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode; display.warning already supports formatted=True. A's three fail_to_pass tests genuinely fail on base (AttributeError on .obj, captured obj is None, TypeError on decrypt(obj=...)). Contradictory family is the stronger structural fit (both designs must own AnsibleError.__init__/message), but the best B motivation is contrived (preserve eager snapshot semantics vs A's laziness), hence low confidence. Complementary family has a real producer/consumer seam (data -> decrypt -> exc.obj) but A's problem statement already claims the vault decode path, so B risks being judged a decomposition; the config-manager locality framing is the most independent angle available. Neither family is ready-made; both need authoring work to be sound.

B is a template-sink feature ticket motivated by the documented webhook template feature (README + funcMap with only `toJson`); a sink user would file it without knowing about the operator fields.
